clue.text: Dancing shoes as means of inflation ?

definitions.meaning: pumps are light slip-on shoes worn for dancing, worn on the foot
a device worked by treading, used to blow up tyres, airbeds or dinghies

explanation.surface: A question whether ballroom slippers might double as something for blowing things up.
explanation.definitionFit: Pumps are the classic light dance slipper, and a pedal-operated air pump for tyres goes by the same two words.

clue.text: In Scotland bridge is out

definitions.meaning: the famous rail and road bridges spanning the Firth near Edinburgh carry this name
onwards and away, as in 'go out' or 'sally out'

explanation.surface: A report that some Scottish bridge has been closed or is down.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish firth gives its name to two celebrated bridges near Edinburgh, and the same word is an old adverb for outwards or onwards.

clue.text: See how they do it at Hurstmonceux

definitions.meaning: to see is to watch or notice

definitions.text: how they do it at Hurstmonceux
definitions.meaning: Herstmonceux Castle in Sussex housed the Royal Greenwich Observatory, whose astronomers watch the sky

explanation.surface: An invitation to come and watch the methods used at a Sussex castle.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Greenwich Observatory moved to Herstmonceux Castle in Sussex after the war, so what is done there is watching the heavens; the clue spells the place Hurstmonceux.
explanation.definitionFit: To see something is to watch or notice it, and an observatory exists to study the stars.

clue.text: That elusive guillotine-cheater

parts.note: points to the hero of Baroness Orczy's novels, the English nobleman who smuggled aristocrats away from the French Revolution's blade and was sought 'here, there, everywhere'

explanation.surface: A description of a slippery figure who keeps people from execution.
explanation.walkthrough: In Orczy's novels the Scarlet hero, named after a small red wildflower, rescues victims of the Terror and famously eludes capture.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scarlet hero of Orczy's novels is the elusive rescuer who cheated the guillotine of its victims.

clue.text: Air. Training Corps's. spell of nautical duty

parts.note: the initials of the Air Training Corps, A, T, C, sit in the centre of a five-letter word meaning to keep guard

explanation.surface: A youth cadet group's period of service at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The Air Training Corps abbreviates to ATC, and those letters form the middle of W-ATC-H; the full stops in the clue are scanning debris, not part of the setter's text.
explanation.definitionFit: At sea the night is split into watches, and the one from midnight to 4 a.m. carries this name.

clue.text: Appeasement upsets RAF officers.

indicators.note: in a down clue upsetting turns the word bottom to top, so these letters read upwards

parts.note: POs are Pilot Officers, a junior commissioned rank in Britain's Royal Air Force

explanation.surface: Giving way to someone annoys senior airmen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upsets' turns POS round to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A sop is a small concession offered to placate someone, which is appeasement in miniature.

clue.text: It's said to be soft-centred-tasty.

indicators.note: soft-centred means the soft thing goes in the centre of the word written beside it

parts.note: P is piano, the musical direction for soft

explanation.surface: A confectioner's boast about a chocolate with a soft filling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's said' looks like a homophone signal, but 'said' is the word itself, with P put in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Sapid is a formal word for having a pleasant flavour, the opposite of insipid.

clue.text: Man's side arm

definitions.meaning: the ... side is the male line of a family, as the distaff side is the female
a weapon, as in 'the right to bear arms'

explanation.surface: A soldier's weapon carried at his side.
explanation.definitionFit: Genealogy calls the male line the spear side, and a lance or javelin is a weapon, an arm.

clue.text: Increases, if split, in 'two

parts.note: cut the first word into two parts, in and creases, and it describes folded fabric

explanation.surface: A puzzle about growth figures that divide into halves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Increases' broken as IN CREASES describes a skirt with folds pressed into it; the comma and apostrophe are scanning marks, the page reads 'if split in two'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fabric that is pressed into folds is in creases, which describes a folded skirt.

clue.text: Does it feature in the breakdown of naval estimates?

definitions.text: Does it feature in the breakdown of naval estimates?

parts.words: Does it feature in the breakdown of naval estimates?
parts.note: a naval budget lists its warships, and a warship class named for wrecking things suits a 'breakdown'

explanation.surface: A question about what appears in the itemised Admiralty budget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breakdown' is an itemised list of costs, but it also suggests destruction, which is what this warship's name says it does.
explanation.definitionFit: A fast escort warship is the kind of item a navy's spending plans list, and its name means a wrecker.

clue.text: Employer went back to sea, started again

indicators.note: going back means the word is written in reverse order

parts.note: one who employs or uses something is a user
the Med is the Mediterranean Sea

explanation.surface: A boss who returned to sailing and took up work afresh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'went back' turns USER into RESU.
explanation.definitionFit: To resume is to begin again after a pause.

clue.text: One whose rhymes 'don't have to be feminine

definitions.text: One whose rhymes 'don't have to be feminine

parts.words: One whose rhymes 'don't have to be feminine
parts.note: a feminine rhyme matches two syllables, but this writer of verse need not use them: she is herself female

explanation.surface: A note on a versifier free of a technical rule about rhymes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'feminine' looks like the prosody term for a two-syllable rhyme; the point is that the writer, a woman, is feminine already. The stray apostrophe is a scanning mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A female writer of verse is the old title for a woman who writes poems.

clue.text: Runyon's Harry in great demand at Bosworth

definitions.meaning: Harry the ... is a gangster in Damon Runyon's Broadway stories
at the Battle of Bosworth Shakespeare's Richard III cries 'my kingdom for a ...!'

explanation.surface: A gangster called Harry was much sought after at a medieval battle.
explanation.definitionFit: Damon Runyon's hoodlum is Harry the Horse, and Richard III offered a kingdom for a mount at Bosworth Field.

clue.text: Simon Bolivar airborne in World War II

definitions.meaning: the South American revolutionary is known as El Libertador, the freer of nations
the Consolidated B-24 was a heavy bomber of the Second World War with this name

explanation.surface: The South American hero took to the skies in the 1940s.
explanation.definitionFit: Bolivar freed much of South America from Spain, and the B-24 bomber flown in the Second World War carried the same title.

clue.text: :Cornish beer oddly: enough in Wales.

indicators.note: oddly enough here says the letters of the preceding words come out in an odd order

explanation.surface: A remark that Cornish ale turns up, strangely, across the Welsh border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly enough' rearranges CORNISH BEER into the old Welsh county; the colons are scanning marks.
explanation.definitionFit: Breconshire was a county of Wales until 1974, so the place lies in that country.

clue.text: Single — so made by marriage?

definitions.meaning: the wedding service says the two shall become ... flesh

explanation.surface: A bachelor wondering whether a wedding makes a pair into a unit.
explanation.definitionFit: A single thing is a lone unit, and the marriage service declares husband and wife a unit of flesh.

clue.text: Iris going underground

parts.note: the part of an iris plant that grows below the soil, dried and used in perfumery

explanation.surface: A flower dying back or a person named Iris taking the Tube.
explanation.walkthrough: Iris can be a woman's name and going underground suggests the London Tube; here it is the plant's underground stem.
explanation.definitionFit: The fragrant dried rhizome of certain irises, used in perfume and gin, is the plant's underground part.

clue.text: Now is the time …

parts.note: the start of a sentence finished by the next clue: the date when people make good promises to themselves

explanation.surface: The opening of a stirring call to act.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs on into 17, '… for good —': the day on which good intentions are traditionally made.
explanation.definitionFit: The first of January is the traditional date for vowing to improve oneself.

clue.text: Roguery of the mysterious Miss Clara

indicators.note: something mysterious is obscured, so the letters of the name are jumbled

explanation.surface: A whodunit hinting at the bad behaviour of an enigmatic lady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mysterious' rearranges MISS CLARA.
explanation.definitionFit: A rascal is a rogue, so behaving like one is roguery.

clue.text: … for good —

parts.note: continues the previous clue: the firm intentions made to reform one's ways

explanation.surface: The end of a call to act once and for all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for good' looks like 'permanently', but read with 15 it means intentions to be good, the promises made on the first of January.
explanation.definitionFit: Firm decisions to behave better are the vows people make at the start of the year.

clue.text: With comparatively bashful exterior a good man makes a bad lawyer

indicators.note: with an exterior means the first word forms the outside wrapped round the other piece
with an exterior means the first word forms the outside wrapped round the other piece

parts.note: more shy is shyer
ST, saint, is crossword shorthand for a good man

explanation.surface: A tale of a timid outward manner hiding a crooked legal practitioner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With … exterior' is the container signal: the bashful comparative goes outside. ST for saint is a crossword convention for a good man.
explanation.definitionFit: A shyster is an unscrupulous lawyer who uses tricky methods.

clue.text: Transport that's about right

parts.note: CA is circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: A vehicle that is roughly suitable.
explanation.definitionFit: A motor vehicle is a means of transport.

clue.text: Authoress allowed entry within French coast

indicators.note: within means one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: cote is French for coast
to let someone in is to allow entry

explanation.surface: A woman writer was admitted to the Riviera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'within' is the container signal. The held text's 'Etna' is a scanning error; the page has no such word, and 'allowed entry' together supplies the inserted piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Colette was the French novelist who wrote Gigi and the Claudine books.

clue.text: Stars in attics?

definitions.meaning: the stars are the lights of the sky
roof windows let daylight into attic rooms

explanation.surface: A question whether celebrities live in lofts.
explanation.definitionFit: Stars are lights of the heavens, and a roof window letting light into a loft has the same name.

clue.text: This bull is always pregnant, said Sir John Mahaffy

definitions.text: This bull is always pregnant, said Sir John Mahaffy

parts.words: This bull is always pregnant, said Sir John Mahaffy
parts.note: the Dublin scholar defined a nonsensical blunder of speech from his country, saying it differed from other bulls by being 'always pregnant'

explanation.surface: A quotation from a Dublin professor about a remarkable animal.
explanation.walkthrough: A bull here is a self-contradictory statement; Mahaffy, Provost of Trinity College Dublin, quipped that the kind from his own country is 'always pregnant', meaning full of meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A ludicrous verbal contradiction is called a bull, and the most famous kind is named after the Emerald Isle.

clue.text: Distribute every book from Genesis to Malachi

parts.note: every means all
the Old Testament (OT) runs from Genesis to Malachi

explanation.surface: Handing out every scripture from the first book to the last of the Hebrew Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: To allot is to share out or assign portions.

clue.text: Changes of courses for those securing 19ac pets

definitions.meaning: a sailing ship changes course by turning into the wind, called going about
19 across is car, and car plus pets makes carpets, fixed down with small nails

explanation.surface: Diversions on the route for people tying up animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A yacht zigzags by tacking, and short broad-headed nails fasten carpets to floors.

clue.text: Exit cue in sketch

parts.note: the way out
an actor's cue is a line of the script

explanation.surface: A stage direction and a prompt in a comic theatre piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sketch' looks like a comic stage act, which fits 'Exit' and 'cue', but here it means a rough drawing.
explanation.definitionFit: A sketch is a rough drawing or summary, giving the main lines only.

clue.text: Oriental lord's antiquity

parts.note: E is east, the Orient
LD is an abbreviation for lord

explanation.surface: The great age of an Eastern nobleman.
explanation.definitionFit: Eld is an archaic word for old age or olden times.

clue.text: Like a.Dostoevsky, or traditional village, character

definitions.text: Like a.Dostoevsky, or traditional village, character

parts.words: Like a.Dostoevsky, or traditional village, character
parts.note: describes both Prince Myshkin, title figure of a Dostoevsky novel, and the simpleton every village was said to have

explanation.surface: A description of someone resembling a Russian novelist's creation or a rural type.
explanation.walkthrough: Dostoevsky's novel The Idiot and the proverbial village idiot both give the character; the full stop is a scanning mark, and the page spells the name Dostoievsky.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Myshkin is the title fool of Dostoevsky, and each village is said to have its fool, so the adjective means foolish.

clue.text: Did its Munich carrier suffer unrequited love ?

definitions.text: Did its Munich carrier suffer unrequited love ?

parts.words: Did its Munich carrier suffer unrequited love ?
parts.note: the flame relayed to the Munich Olympics was carried by runners, and one who carries a flame for someone loves in vain

explanation.surface: A question whether the runner bringing something to Munich was lovesick.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'carry a torch' for someone is to love them without return, and an Olympic flame was carried to Munich in 1972.
explanation.definitionFit: The Olympic flame is carried in a hand-held light, and loving someone hopelessly is called carrying one.

clue.text: Unlike the sleep of-Joel's old men

definitions.text: Unlike the sleep of-Joel's old men

parts.words: Unlike the sleep of-Joel's old men
parts.note: the prophet Joel promises 'your old men shall dream dreams', so sleep unlike theirs is free of visions

explanation.surface: A reference to the slumber of elderly men in a book of the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: Joel 2:28 says 'your old men shall dream dreams', so a sleep unlike theirs has none.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleep without any visions is the opposite of what Joel foresees for the old.
